items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: as you know I had a quartet at one time with Mariano and so on

ctx.x: Yeah, I think at that point I had ten years before that before I came to this country, I had ten years of my career in Japan. And I was doing pretty okay, I got to the point where I was playing probably faster than anybody and longer than anybody. That’s the whole thing. But a big band was something that I wasn’t quite interested in. I was interested in the individual players. I was mainly, and more than anything I was interested in my piano playing to be improved a little more. I sort of thought I could, and I…

became interested in writing much, much later, perhaps ’67, around there. Actually in ’67 I had my own concert, my own produced, to try and get money for work and so on, at the Town Hall and at that time I thought, I was hoping that if some people noticed me, and I had a solo and trio, and about four big band charts. And when I was rehearsing that I felt that’s what I wanted to do. I felt like that’s what I wanted to do. Because up to that point I was getting a little bit of anxiety about the fact that, as you…

That’s an interesting statement. I mean you certainly made an impact and kept that tradition alive. You know when you read about your music, most people mention that it brings in a whole other area of influence from your native culture. And when you write do you consciously try to think of things from your youth that are now combined with American jazz, or is it just kind of part of you?

items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And that … we moved to New Jersey. And we formed a quartet.

ctx.x: Uh, well, you married Charlie Mariano.
